Assuming that on an average, one out of ${10}^{3}$ photons incident on the ball is able to eject an electron, then the potential of the sphere will be
questions.solution:
The total number of photons striking the surface of the ball is

${n}_{p} = \dfrac{Eλ}{hc} = \dfrac{1 \times {10}^{- 7} \times 200 \times {10}^{- 9}}{6 .6 \times {10}^{- 34} \times 3 \times {10}^{8}} = 1 \times {10}^{11}$

The total number of electrons ejected is

${n}_{e} = \dfrac{1{0}^{11}}{1{0}^{3}} = 1{0}^{8}$

$∴ V = \dfrac{q}{4{πε}_{0}r} = \dfrac{\left({10}^{8} \times 1 .6 \times {10}^{- 19}\right) \times 9 \times {10}^{9}}{4 .8 \times {10}^{- 2}} = 3V$

questions.q: The P.E. ' $U$ ' of a moving particle of mass ' $m$ ' varies with ' $\mathrm{x}$ ' is shown in the figure. The de-Broglie wavelength of the particle in the regions $0 \leq x \leq 1$ and $x>1$ are $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ respectively. If the total energy of the particle is ' $\mathrm{nE}$ ', then the ratio $\lambda_1 / \lambda_2$ is
questions.solution: In the region $0 \leq x \leq 1$, the potential energy of the particle is $E$. Total energy is $\mathrm{nE}$. Hence, kinetic energy, $\mathrm{K}=\mathrm{nE}-\mathrm{E}=(\mathrm{n}-1) \mathrm{E}$ Its momentum, $\mathrm{p}_1=\sqrt{2 \mathrm{mK}}=\sqrt{2 \mathrm{~m}(\mathrm{n}-1) \mathrm{E}}$ \therefore \lambda_1=$\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\mathrm{p}_1}=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\sqrt{2 \mathrm{~m}(\mathrm{n}-1) \mathrm{E}}}$In the region $\mathrm{x}>1, \mathrm{PE}$ is zero Hence, total is kinetic energy. $\begin{aligned}$& \therefore $\mathrm{K}=\mathrm{nE}$\\ & \therefore \lambda_2=$\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\mathrm{p}_2}=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\sqrt{2 \mathrm{mnE}}}$\\ & \therefore $\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}=\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{n}}{\mathrm{n}-1}} \end{aligned}$

questions.q: The maximum kinetic energy of a photoelectron liberated from the surface of lithium with work function $2.35 \mathrm{eV}$ by electromagnetic radiation whose electric component varies with time as : $E=a\left[1+\cos \left(2 \pi f_1 t\right)\right] \cos 2 \pi f_2 t$ (where $a$ is a constant $)$ is \left(f_1=3.6 \times 10^{15} \mathrm{~Hz}\right.$, and $f_2=1.2 \times 10^{15} \mathrm{~Hz}$ and Planck's constant  \left.h=6.6 \times 10^{-34} \mathrm{Js}\right)$
questions.solution: Here, work function, $W_0=2.35 \mathrm{eV}$ and the electric component of electromagnetic radiation $\begin{aligned}$& E=a\left[$1+\cos \left($2 $\pi$f_1 t\right)\right] \cos \left($2 $\pi$f_2 t\right) \\ \text{ and } \Rightarrow E=\left[$a \cos \left($2 $\pi$f_2 t\right)+a \cos \left($2 $\pi$f_1 t\right) \cos \left($2 $\pi$f_2 t\right)\right] \\ \text{ and } \left(\because \cos$A \cos B=$\frac{1}{2}[\cos ($A+B)-\cos (A-B))\right. \\ & \Rightarrow E=a \cos \left($2 $\pi$f_2 t\right)+$\frac{a}{2} \cos$2 $\pi\left($f_1+f_2\right) t-$\frac{a}{2} \cos$2 $\pi\left($f_1-f_2\right) t \end{aligned} So, the electric component has 3 sub-components with frequencies are, f_2,  \left($f_1+f_2\right)$\text { and }\left($f_1-f_2\right) So, for maximum kinetic energy of photoelectron, we take photon of maximum frequency. Hence, $\begin{aligned}$E_{\max } \text{ and } =$\frac{h v_{\max }}{e}=\frac{6.6 \times 10^{-34} \times\left(3.6 \times 10^{15}+1.2 \times 10^{15}\right)}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}}$\\ \text{ and } =19.8 $\mathrm{eV} \end{aligned}$Hence, the maximum kinetic energy, $\mathrm{KE}_{\text {max }}=$E_{\text {max }}-W_0=19.8-2.35=17.45 $\mathrm{eV}Hence, the correct option is (d).$

questions.q: A charged particle is accelerated from rest through a certain potential difference. The de-Broglie wavelength is $\lambda_1$ when it is accelerated through $V_1$ and is $\lambda_2$ when accelerated through $V_2$. The ratio $\lambda_1 / \lambda_2$ is
questions.solution:
The de-Broglie wavelength associated with a charged particle is given by \lambda=$\frac{h}{\sqrt{m q V}}$where, $h=$ planck's constant
$m=$ mass of charged particle
$q=$ charge on the particle
$V=$ potential at which the charged particle is accelerated.
$\therefore$
\lambda_1=$\frac{h}{\sqrt{m_1 q V_1}}, \lambda_2=$\frac{h}{\sqrt{m_2 q V_2}}$Here, $\begin{aligned}$m_1 & =m_2 \\
$\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}$& =$\sqrt{\frac{m_2 q V_2}{m_1 q V_1}}=\sqrt{\frac{V_2}{V_1}}$\\
& =V_2^{\frac{1}{2}} $\cdotV_1^{\frac{1}{2}}
\end{aligned}

questions.q:
Photoelectric effect supports quantum nature of light because,

1. There is a minimum frequency of light below which, no photoelectrons are emitted.

2. Electric charge of photoelectrons is quantized.

3. Maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons depends only on the frequency of light and not on its intensity.

4. Even when metal surface is faintly illuminated, the photoelectrons leave the surface immediately.

questions.q: Two particles $A$ and $B$ of same mass have their de-Broglie wavelengths in the ratio ${X}_{A}: {X}_{B} = K: 1 .$ Their potential energies ${U}_{A}: {U}_{B} = 1: K^{2} .$ The ratio of their total energies ${E}_{A}: {E}_{B}$ is
questions.solution:
According to question, $\dfrac{{X}_{A}}{{X}_{B}} = \dfrac{K}{1}$ ...(i)

$\dfrac{{U}_{A}}{{U}_{B}} = \dfrac{1}{K^{2}}$

So, ${U}_{A} = y$ and ${U}_{B} = K^{2}y$

According to de-Broglie wavelength,

$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2m{K}_{1}}}$ .....(ii)

Here, ${K}_{1}$ is kinetic energy.

So, from Equations (i) and (ii),

$⇒ \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2m{K}_{1A}}}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2m{K}_{1B}}}\right)} = \dfrac{K}{1} ⇒ \sqrt{\dfrac{{K}_{1B}}{{K}_{1A}}} = \dfrac{K}{1}$

$⇒ \dfrac{{K}_{1B}}{{K}_{1A}} = K^{2}$

So, ${K}_{1B} = K^{2}x$ and ${K}_{1A} = x$

$∵$ Total energy, $E = {K}_{1} + U$

So, ${E}_{A} = {K}_{1A} + {U}_{A}$

and ${E}_{B} = {K}_{1B} + {U}_{B}$

or $\dfrac{{E}_{A}}{{E}_{B}} = \dfrac{{K}_{1A} + {U}_{A}}{{K}_{1B} + {U}_{B}} = \dfrac{x + y}{K^{2}x + K^{2}y}$

$⇒$ So, $\dfrac{{E}_{A}}{{E}_{B}} = \dfrac{1}{K^{2}}\left(or\right){E}_{A}: {E}_{B} = 1: K^{2}$

questions.q: When certain metal surface is illuminated with a light of wavelength $\lambda$ , the stopping potential is V, when the same surface is illuminated by light of wavelength $2\lambda$ , the stopping potential is  \left(\dfrac{V}{3}\right)$ . The threshold wavelength for the surface is$
questions.solution:
Given for a metal, wavelength of light used = $\lambda$ stopping potential =V
If ${\lambda}_{0}$ be the threshold wavelength, then maximum kinetic energy of emitted electrons
${K}_\max = hc \left(\dfrac{1}{\lambda} - \dfrac{1}{{\lambda}_{0}}\right) …(i)
Again, wavelength of used light
${\lambda}^{'} = 2\lambda$
Stopping potential, V’ $= $\dfrac{V}{3}
then ${K}_\max = hc \left(\dfrac{1}{\lambda}, \dfrac{1}{{\lambda}_{0}}\right)$
$⇒ eV^{'}hc \left(\dfrac{1}{2\lambda} - \dfrac{1}{{\lambda}_{0}}\right)
$⇒ $\dfrac{eV}{3} =$hc \left(\dfrac{1}{2\lambda}, \dfrac{1}{{\lambda}_{0}}\right)$ …. (ii)
From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we have
$\dfrac{eV}{\dfrac{eV}{3}} = \dfrac{hc\left(\dfrac{1}{\lambda} - \dfrac{1}{{\lambda}_{0}}\right)}{hc\left(\dfrac{1}{2\lambda}, \dfrac{1}{{\lambda}_{0}}\right)}$
$3\left(\dfrac{1}{2\lambda} - \dfrac{1}{{\lambda}_{0}}\right) = \dfrac{1}{\lambda} - \dfrac{1}{{\lambda}_{0}}$
$⇒ {\lambda}_{0} = 4\lambda$
So, threshold wavelength is 4 times of wavelength of ligh.

Given that~$2 %$of the incident,~photons produce photoelectron therefore, number of photoelectrons produced by photons~is~$= \dfrac{2}{100} \times 1 . 51 \times {10}^{20}m^{- 2}s^{- 1}$

Now, the number of photoelectrons emitted from an area of $2{cm}^{2}$ of the surface in~$1s$is nearly~

$n = \left(1s\right)\left(2 \times {10}^{- 4}m^{2}\right) \times \left(3 . 02 \times {10}^{18}m^{- 2}s^{- 1}\right)n = 6 . 04 \times {10}^{14}$

questions.q: An electron of mass $m$ and magnitude of charge $e$ at rest, gets accelerated by a constant electric field $E$. The rate of change of de-Broglie wavelength of this electron at a time $t$ is (ignore relativistic effects)
questions.solution:
The acceleration of the electron is

$a = \dfrac{eE}{m}$

The velocity of the electron as a function of time is

$v = at = \dfrac{eE}{m}t$

The de-Broglie wavelength is

$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv}$

$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{m\left(\dfrac{eE}{m}\right)t}$

$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{eEt}$
$\dfrac{d\lambda}{dt} = - \dfrac{h}{eEt^{2}}$

questions.q: Two electrons in two hydrogen-like atoms& $A$ and $B$~have their total energies ${E}_{A}$ and ${E}_{B}$ in the ratio ${E}_{A}: {E}_{B} = 1: 2$ . Their potential energies ${U}_{A}$ and ${U}_{B}$ are in the ratio ${U}_{A}: {U}_{B} = 1: 2$ . If ${\lambda}_{A}$ and ${\lambda}_{B}$ are their de-Broglie wavelengths, then ${\lambda}_{A}: {\lambda}_{B}$ is
questions.solution:
Given,

$\dfrac{{E}_{A}}{{E}_{B}} = \dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{{U}_{A}}{{U}_{B}} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

So ${E}_{A} = x, {E}_{B} = 2x$

And ${U}_{A} = y, {U}_{B} = 2y$

$∵ {E}_{A} = {U}_{A} + {K}_{A}$

And ${E}_{B} = {U}_{B} + {K}_{B}$

here ${K}_{A}$ and ${K}_{B}$ are kinetic energy of particles $A$ and $B$

So ${K}_{A} = {E}_{A} - {U}_{A} = \left(x - y\right)$ .....(i)

${K}_{B} = {E}_{B} - {U}_{B} = 2 \left(x - y\right)$ ....(ii)

$∵$ de-Broglie wavelength,

$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mk}}$

So ${\lambda}_{A} = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2m{K}_{A}}}, {\lambda}_{B} = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2m{K}_{B}}}$

$∴ \dfrac{{\lambda}_{A}}{{\lambda}_{B}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{{K}_{B}}{{K}_{A}}} .....($iii)

From Equation (i), (ii) and (iii),

$\dfrac{{\lambda}_{A}}{{\lambda}_{B}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2\left(x - y\right)}{\left(x - y\right)}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{1}$

questions.q: A perfectly reflecting solid hemisphere of radius& $R$~is placed in the path of a parallel beam of light of large aperture. If the beam carries an intensity~$I$, find the force exerted by the beam on the hemisphere.
questions.solution:
Let& $O$ be the centre of the sphere and~$OZ$~be the line possible to the incident beam (diagram). Consider a radius $OP$~of the sphere making an angle $\text{\theta}$ with~$OZ$. Rotate this radius about~$OZ$~to get another circle on the sphere. Change $\text{\theta}$ to $\text{\theta} + d\text{\theta}$ and rotate the radius about~$OZ$~to get another circle on the sphere. The part of the sphere between these circles is a ring of area $2\pir^{2}sin\text{\theta}d\text{\theta}$. Consider a small part of $\Delta A$ of this ring at$P$.~The energy~of the light falling on this part in time $\Delta t$ is,

$\Delta U = I \Delta t \left(\Delta$A cos $\text{\theta}\right)

The momentum of this light falling on \Delta$A$ is \Delta \dfrac{U}{c} along~$QP$. The light is reflected by the sphere along~$PR$. The change in the momentum, along the inward normal, is,

\Delta$p = 2$\dfrac{\Delta U}{c}$cos$\text{\theta} = \dfrac{2}{c}$I $\Delta$t \left(\Delta A\cos^{2}\text{\theta}\right)$

The force on $\Delta A$ due to the light falling on it is,

$\dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{2}{c}I \Delta A\cos^{2}\text{\theta}$

The force is along~$PO$. The resultant force on the ring as well as on the sphere is along~$ZO$, by symmetry. The component of the force on $\Delta A$ along~$ZO$~is,

$\dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}cos\theta = \dfrac{2}{c}I \Delta A\cos^{2}\theta$

The force acting on the ring is,

$dF = \dfrac{2}{c}I\left(2\pir^{2}sin\text{\theta}d\text{\theta}\right)\cos^{3}\text{\theta}$

The force on the entire sphere is,

$F = \mathop{∫}_{0}^{\pi / 2}\dfrac{4\pir^{2}I}{c}\cos^{3}\theta sin\text{\theta}d\text{\theta}$

$= - \mathop{∫}_{0}^{\pi / 2}\dfrac{4\pir^{2}I}{c}\cos^{3}\text{\theta}d \left($cos$\text{\theta}\right)

$= - \mathop{∫}_{\text{\theta} =$0}^{\pi$/ $2}\dfrac{4\$pir^{2}I}{c}{\dfrac{\cos^{4}\text{\t$theta}}{4}}_{0}^{\pi$/ 2} = $\dfrac{\pir^{2}I}{c}

Note that integration is done only for the hemisphere, that faces the incident beam.

$

questions.q: A photon of wavelength $\lambda$ is absorbed by an electron confined to a box of length $\sqrt{\dfrac{35h\lambda}{8mc}}$.~As a result, the electron makes a transition from state, $k = 1$~to~the state $n$.~Subsequently, the electron transits from the state~$n$ to the state~$m$ by emitting a photon of wavelength,~${λ}^{'} = 1 . 75\lambda$.& Then,
questions.solution:
Let the length of confined box be,& $l = \sqrt{\dfrac{35h\lambda}{8mc}}$.

Kinetic energy of electron after absorbing photon,~$K = \dfrac{hc}{λ}$.

The de-Broglie wavelength of electron with this kinetic energy is given as,~${λ}_{deBroglie} = \dfrac{h}{2mK} = \dfrac{h}{2m\left(\dfrac{hc}{λ}\right)} = \sqrt{\dfrac{h\lambda}{2mc}}$.

Now, number of loops formed in the confined length is given as,

$p = l\left(\dfrac{\lambdadeBroglie}{2}\right) = \dfrac{2l}{\lambdadeBroglie} ⇒ p = \dfrac{2 \times \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{35h\lambda}{8mc}\right)}}{\left(\dfrac{h\lambda}{2mc}\right)} = \sqrt{35} \approx 6$

Electron forms~$n$~loops in~$n^{th}$~orbit. Hence, the required number of states of the electron after absorbing photon is~$n = 6$. This is present& only in one option.

options: Statements I, II and III are true
Statements I, II are true, but statement III is false
Statements II, III are true, but statement I is false
Statements I, II and III are false

So, (III) is in correct.

questions.q: A particle $X$ of mass $m$~and initial velocity $u$ collide with another particle $Y$ of mass $\dfrac{3m}{4}$ which is at rest, The collision is head on and perfectly elastic. The ratio of de-Broglie wavelengths ${λ}_{Y}$~and ${λ}_{X}$ after the collision is
questions.solution:
For perfectly elastic collision,

total momentum before collision $=$ total momentum after collision

i.e. $m \cdot u + \dfrac{3m}{4} \times 0 = m{v}_{x} + \dfrac{3m}{4} \cdot {v}_{y}$

$⇒ 4u = 4{v}_{x} + 3{v}_{y} . . . \left(i\right)$

Coefficient of restitution,

$e = $\dfrac{Velocityof seperation \left({v}_{y} - {v}_{x}\right)aftercollision}{Velocityof approach \left({u}_{x} - {u}_{y}\right)beforecollision}

$⇒ 1 = $\dfrac{{v}_{y} - {v}_{x}}{u - 0}~ ~[$∵ {u}_{x} = v$~and~${u}_{y} = 0$]

$u = {v}_{y} - {v}_{x} . . . \left(ii\right)$

Solving Equations. (i) and (ii), we have

${v}_{x} = \dfrac{u}{7}$~and~${u}_{y} = \dfrac{8u}{7}$

$∴ \dfrac{\lambday}{\lambdax} = \dfrac{h / m{v}_{y}}{h / \dfrac{3m}{4} \cdot {v}_{x}} = \dfrac{3}{4} \cdot \dfrac{vx}{vy} = \dfrac{3}{4} \cdot \dfrac{u / 7}{8u / 7} = \dfrac{3}{32}$

The Einstein's equation for photoelectric effect : $K{E}_\max = \dfrac{hc}{λ} - W$~where,

$W = \dfrac{hc}{λ} - e{V}_{0} = \dfrac{ \left(6 . 62 \times {10}^{- 34}\right) \times \left(3 \times {10}^{8}\right)}{1240 \times {10}^{- 10}} - \left(1 . 6 \times {10}^{- 19}\right)\left(8\right)$
$= 3 . 2 \times {10}^{- 19} =2$ eV as~ \left(1eV = 1 . 6 \times {10}^{- 19}\right)$

If ${λ}_{0}$ be the threshold wavelength, $W = $\dfrac{hc}{\lambda0}

${λ}_{0} = $\dfrac{hc}{W} = \dfrac{6 . 62 \times {10}^{- 34} \times 3 \times {10}^{8}}{3 . 2 \times {10}^{- 19}} =$6 . 2 \times {10}^{- 7}m = 6200A °$

$

questions.q: Light of two different frequencies whose photons have energies $1$ eV and $2.5$ eV, respectively, successively illuminate a metallic surface whose work function is $0.5$ eV. The ratio of maximum speeds of the emitted electrons will be
questions.solution:
According to Einstein's photoelectric equation, the maximum kinetic energy of emitted photoelectrons is ${K}_\max = hν - {ϕ}_{0}$

Where $hν$ is the energy of the incident photon and ${ϕ}_{0}$ is the work function.

But ${K}_\max = \dfrac{1}{2}m{v}_\max^{2}$

$∴ \dfrac{1}{2}m{v}_\max^{2} = hν - {ϕ}_{0}$

As per the question,

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}\max_{1} ⁡ = 1eV - \text{0.5}eV = \text{0.5}eV$ ...(i)

and $\dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}\max_{2} ⁡ = \text{2.5}eV - \text{0.5}eV = 2eV$ ...(ii)

Dividing equation (i) by equation (ii), we get

$\dfrac{v^{2}\max_{1} ⁡}{v^{2}\max_{2} ⁡} = \dfrac{\text{0.5}eV}{2eV} = \dfrac{1}{4}$

$\dfrac{{v}_{\max_{1} ⁡}}{{v}_{\max_{2} ⁡}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{4}} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

For $0 \le x \le 1$ , the de-Broglie wavelength is ${λ}_{1}$ and for $x > 1$ the de-Broglie wavelength is ${λ}_{2}$. The total energy of the particle is $2{E}_{0}$. Find $\dfrac{{λ}_{1}}{{λ}_{2}}$
questions.solution:
For $0 \le x \le 1$ , $U = {E}_{0}$

$∴$ Kinetic energy, ${K}_{1}$ = Total energy - $U$

$= 2{E}_{0} - {E}_{0} = {E}_{0}$
$∴ {λ}_{1} = \dfrac{h}{2m{E}_{0}}$

For $x > 1$, $U = 0$

$∴$ Kinetic energy ${K}_{2}$ = Total energy -$U$

$= 2{E}_{0}$

$∴ {λ}_{2} = \dfrac{h ⁡}{\sqrt{2 m ⁡ {( 2\text{E} ⁡}_{0} )}}$ ...(ii)

From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we have

$\dfrac{{λ}_{1}}{{λ}_{2}} = \sqrt{2}$

questions.q: A photocell is illuminated by a point source of light, which is placed at a distance $d$ from the cell. If the distance becomes $\dfrac{d}{2}$, then number of electrons emitted per second will
questions.solution:
The number of electrons emitted per second is known as the intensity of the light. Intensity is given by,& $I = \dfrac{E}{4\pir^{2}t}$, where~$E$~is the energy of the source,~$r$~is the distance and~$t$~is the time.

We can see that the intensity of the incident light is~inversely proportional to the square of the distance.

When~$r = d$,~${I}_{1} = \dfrac{E}{4\pid^{2}t}$.

When~$r = \dfrac{d}{2}$,~${I}_{2} = \dfrac{E}{4\pi\left(\dfrac{d}{2}\right)2t}$.

We have~${I}_{2} = 4{I}_{1}$. Therefore, intensity becomes four times which means the number of electrons will become four times.

questions.solution: Given, wavelength of incident radiation, \(\lambda=400 $\mathrm{~nm}=$4 $\times$10^{-7} $\mathrm{~m}$\) electric field, \(E=2 $\mathrm{~N}$/ $\mathrm{C}$\) and distance, \(s=1 $\mathrm{~m}$\) \(\therefore\) Energy of the incident light, \(\begin{aligned}E \text{ and } =\frac{h c}{\lambda}=\frac{6.6 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^8}{4 \times 10^{-7}}\\ \text{ and } =4.95 $\times$10^{-19} $\mathrm{~$J}=\frac{4.95 \times 10^{19}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}}$\\ $\mathrm{~J}$ \text{ and } =3.09 \simeq 3 $\mathrm{leV} \end{aligned}$\) If \(a\) be the retardation of emitted electrons in the electric field, then, \(\quad a=\frac{q E}{m}\) initial speed \(u\) of emitted electron is calculated as \(v²=u²-2 a s \Rightarrow 0=u²-2 a $\times$1 \Rightarrow u²=2 a=\frac{2 q E}{m}\) \(\therefore\) Maximum kinetic energy of the electron, \$(\begin{aligned}$ \text{ and } K_{\max }=$\frac{1}{2}$m u²=m $\cdot \frac{2 q E}{m}=$q E=1.6 $\times$10^{-19} $\times$2 \\ \text{ and } K_{\max }=3.2 $\times$10^{-19} $\mathrm{~J}=$2 $\mathrm{eV} \end{aligned}$\) \(\therefore\) Work function of the surface, \(W_0=E-K_{\max }=3.1-2=1.1 $\mathrm{eV}$\)
